blocks.x: Today is Sunday, June 14th, 1959. This is Brian Rust of London, England. I'm sitting in the living room of Nick LaRocca's home, 2218 Constance Street, New Orleans, Louisiana. Mr LaRocca has done me the honour of making a tape recording of his voice telling his story of how he came to create jazz and his opinions and the whole story of the growth of the music. And he's asked me to give my side of it, how I came to be interested in the music and what it means to me and to English people now. Until 1936, I'd never heard of the original Dixieland jazz band. That year, on March 31st to be exact, I happened to discover in a London second-hand shop a copy, in very bad condition indeed, of At the Jazz Band Ball and Ostrich Walk on his master's voice record. It was one which had been made in New York in 1918. I'd never heard of the band and I took the record home. It cost exactly one penny. And I took the record home and played it and immediately I realised that I'd got something quite different from the ordinary dance music and popular music of the day, which interested me as far as it went. But this was something quite different. This was a new thing entirely, although it was then 18 years old. I made some enquiries and discovered that this was not the only record that the original Dixieland jazz band had made. But I was very upset to find that there wasn't one single record then in the catalogue that I could buy in brand new condition and so enjoy to the full. About six months later, without my asking for it, his master's voice reissued the famous original Tiger Rag. And I promptly bought that and they backed it up with Jasmine Blues, which again was the first recording of that number. And then a few months later still they issued some more. And although I didn't know it at the time, Mr. La Rocca had regrouped the original band and was in fact in 1936 itself recording some of the old numbers again under the modern electric system. And they were issued in England too. At least four of them were. Tiger Rag, Skeleton Jangle, original Dixieland One Step and Barnyard Blues. And of course, as soon as I realised they were on sale, I snapped them up. Well, of course, from there on, I started looking round for the real rarities. But being a schoolboy, I didn't have very much money to spare and I had to wait until I started work in 1940. And I started advertising for records and getting to know other collectors. And in fact, I started my expanding my circle of friends by answering an advertisement in the London Gramophone publication of June 1940. Because there was an advertisement in that which said, wanted records by the original Dixieland Jazz Band will buy them. And they followed an address which I wrote to. And we started comparing notes and one thing led to another. And I met another fellow who collected the records and who had nearly all of them. And including the 12-inch Columbias, which the band made in London in 1919 and 1920. And a bit later on, I discovered some of these for myself. And within about five years, I managed to get all of them, except the Aerelean Vocalians, which I still don't have. And one or two of the OKs, which I've managed to get since. Although, of course, the OKs were not made by the original band. They had Artie Seberg on clarinet and Henry Vanicelli on piano. A little while later, I presented a program on the air, two copies of which I've given to Mr. La Rocka, dealing with the influence of the original Dixieland Jazz Band on other bands. Some of them I put in for the sheer fun of the thing, because the bands were obviously striving to capture the spirit and the letter of the original jazz music without getting very far with it. Others made quite a good job of it. I featured records in this program of Muggsy Spanier and Sam Lannin and Bix Beiderbecq. And, generally speaking, the program was quite successful. Although, of course, having met Mr. La Rocka since, I've learned a great deal more about the truth of the origins of jazz than I knew at the time of making the broadcast. That was in 1954. In 1957, Columbia Graphophone Company in London asked me to lend them the original 12-inch recordings, because they wanted to transfer them to long-playing records and issue them on the market again, because they thought there would be a demand for them. And they were right. There was. All my copies were in perfect condition, and they made a very good transfer process. I sent a copy of the finished record to Mr. La Rocka, and he was very pleased with it. I wrote the sleeve note too, the liner note for it. And I'm afraid that a number of the facts that I put in there weren't facts at all. They were just the things that other people who knew less about the subject than I did had told me. And I received a letter from Mr. La Rocka in November 1957, putting me really wise on this subject. I really got the full details. And ever since then, I've had a stream of correspondence from him with the most wonderful enclosures, most of which are in the archives of the Tulane University. They were press cuttings, letters from musicians and important people, theatre bills, record supplements, and even pieces of music which had never been published. And this, of course, I very much appreciate. They occupy a very treasured place in my own library. Although I came to New Orleans in 1951, for one reason or another, I didn't get around to seeing Mr. La Rocka. There were certain people here who should be nameless, who deflected me from seeing him because they said that he wouldn't be of any interest in me. I ought to go and hear the real thing which amounted to a collection of very third-rate, or even ninth-rate musicians and old-timers who were leftovers from the ragtime and marching band era, which may have been all right in its time, but they can't play jazz. They just don't play jazz, let's face it. There's a very prevalent rumour going around that, in fact, it's a famous story perpetrated by numbers of writers and so-called historians in jazz, that the original Creole jazz, if that's the word, orchestra, under the direction of Freddie Kepard, recorded for Victor before the original Dixieland jazz band did. That is not so. When I was in New York last week, I was privileged to inspect the files of RCA Victor, the company which, so legend has it, made these records. They certainly made the original Dixieland jazz band records in February 1917, and I've checked on that and found that is so. In fact, everything that Mr. Larrakus told me ties in with the Victor files. I've gone into this thing very thoroughly, so I know exactly that everything he says is true. And when I was going through the volume of 1918 recordings, that is, the year after the first original Dixieland jazz band records, I found an entry which is rather interesting. Under the heading of Monday, December the 2nd, 1918, that is, nearly two years after the first original Dixieland jazz band recordings, I found an entry under the heading of the original Creole jazz band. It didn't give any names. It simply gave the instruments. I forget exactly what they were, but there was cornet, trombone, clarinet, piano, mandolin, I think, and drums, and one title, Tackin' Them Down, I think it was called. And it was described as a test record made for trial purposes, and it was stamped, Master Destroyed, Rejected. I made further inquiries to see if the record was available, to see what it sounded like. It was told that it was considered unsuitable for issue, and had long ago been destroyed, and that what the file said was true. There was no further reference to the original Creole jazz band, or in fact any other jazz band, apart from the Louisiana Five, and that was some time later on still. The only jazz band making records for Victor, or Columbia, because I inspected Columbia's files also, at that time, in fact between any time up to 1922 or 23, was the original Dixieland jazz band. There were no others. There were a number of copyists. There was Earl Fuller's so-called jazz band. Well, of course, we all have heard records of those, and we know exactly how unlike the original Dixieland jazz band they were. There was Ted Lewis's jazz band on Columbia, which was no more a jazz band than the Boston Promenade Orchestra. And there were a number of other complete phonies, let's say. There were no other genuine jazz bands on record at that time. I've inspected not only the Victor and Columbia files, but also those of the Edison Company, and of those of the Jeanette Company, the Star Piano Company of Richmond. I've inspected the OK files of the General Phonograph Corporation of New York. All these have been made available to me through the courtesy of the parent companies concerned. And most of the other famous recording companies, like Capitol and Decca, weren't even in existence at that time, let alone making records of jazz. So I would like to put on record the fact that in 1917, and from then on until 1922 or 1923, there is no trace whatever of any band having made jazz recordings, except the original Dixieland jazz band. And they made quite a large number, though for my money not enough. It's a great pity that certain of them, which are listed in the files as rejected, were never issued. I don't know whether the masters are still available. I imagine they can't be. But there was a Satanic Blues, there was a Lassie's Candy, and there was a tune called In the Dusk, none of which were ever published. And there were various alternative takes of the numbers that were published, which we don't seem to have had. Nevertheless, I'm more than delighted to be able to meet Mr. La Rocca, and to see his wonderful collection of press cuttings and all the other things, pictures, many of which have never been, never appeared in public before. And I'm looking forward very much to reading the book which my good friend Harry Brunn has written on the subject, because this will put the record straight once and for all. He's been into this question, I believe, for the last 20 years, so it should be a wonderful job of work. I can quite understand the difficulties that he was up against when he tried to get the book published before, because most publishers, so he tells me, wouldn't look at it, because it refused steadfastly to mention people like Buddy Bolden, who was put in the Louisiana State Asylum, I believe, in 1905 or thereabouts. And in that connection, incidentally, I've done a little research as well. I've done some technical work on his so-called recordings. He's supposed to have made some records, I believe cylinders or discs, some people say they were discs, before he was put in the loony bin in the crazy house. Well, he may have done. One thing is certainly he didn't make any flat discs, because I've been right the way through the Victor and Columbia files again. They were the only companies in existence at that time. And I've been through their files right the way back to 1900 when the firms began, and there is no sign of any records of Buddy Bolden. So much for the discs. It's absolutely unthinkable that any other company could have made discs at that time, because there just weren't any companies. They owned, the Victor and Columbia owned the patent rights to making disc records. Anybody else making them would have been stamped on at once. Nobody would have had that much financial backing in any case. So we know they can't have been discs that Mr Bolden had made. He may have made some private cylinders, but there again, if he did, it would be quite impossible, even if we found them nowadays, to play them. So that I think it's fair to say that his prowess, if any, must remain a beautiful legend, a fairy story designed for credulous people ready to believe that sort of thing. What we have got are recordings, which anyone can play, of the original Dixieland jazz band, and that's good enough. All right, so they weren't made in 1900, they were made in 1917. Never mind. They were good enough, and good enough for anybody to listen to. They're jazz, that's what matters, and they're the first jazz. And until then, there was no jazz. There was ragtime, yes. There were ragtime piano rolls, there were a few ragtime recordings. But there were a few recordings by coloured bands. There was Jim Europe on Victor, there was Wilbur Sweatman on Columbia, there was Ford Dabney on a number of different labels, mostly Aeolian and Vecalian. But one's only got to listen to those. They're not easy, they're not difficult to find.

it's easy enough to listen to them. I've only got to listen to those and compare them with the original Dixieland Jazz Band to realise that the one is Ragtime and the other is Jazz. The original Dixieland Jazz Band isn't called Jazz for Nothing. There are other musicians having laid claim to having made the first jazz records. I have just compiled a book which lays great stress on the dates of recordings. The first jazz recordings in the book, not Ragtime, the first jazz recordings, are those by the original Dixieland Jazz Band. Wilbur Swetman came some time afterwards, so did Earl Fuller, so did Ted Lewis. The bands that came before that are Ragtime bands. There was Sousa's band, there was Arthur Pryor's band, they all played Ragtime. If you doubt that, read Rudy Blesch's book of that name, they all played Ragtime. He gives a great deal of space to describing Sousa's band when they played Ragtime. And to the banjoists like Vess Osman, they played Ragtime. They didn't play jazz though. They played Ragtime. It was all written down and they played everything as written. They couldn't do otherwise. They weren't fakers. They couldn't play. They hadn't got any invention at all in them. They played what was written and that was that. It may have been good or it may have been bad. We're not concerned with that at this date. This was Ragtime. It was played off the score. Jazz was played as the musicians felt under the directorship of my good friend here, Mr. La Rocca. Well, I don't think there's anything much else I can say except that this has been a really great privilege to me and there's only one thing that I wish, that is I could stay longer here in this wonderful city. The only thing I hate about New Orleans is leaving it.
Can I ask you a question, Mr. Rust? Certainly. You remember me writing you and telling you that every colored and white band from New Orleans had their chance? Oh, yes.
And they all failed?
Yes. In the beginning, I don't think you believe me, but you've checked this now, haven't you?
I have, yes. Yes, I believe you.

So you found every word that I have told you is the truth? Absolutely. Now they're going around today taking tape recordings of men who never went out as far as Calton Avenue. That's just not even the city line.
Uh-huh.

And they're saying there was some part of the creation of jazz. That Jack Lane, who played a drum and lousy drums at that, created jazz. Now that's good enough for men who thrive on thievery, on a word that we had nothing to do. Our jazz was started in Chicago. We took in the ragtime and changed the rhythm in Chicago. In 1916, we seen we were going to be a flop the first night. And I, being a good dancer, I watched those people. At that time, they had Vernon Castle doing the castle walk. And everybody was trying to copy them. It was a single step. And I'd come to my mind, let me play one of them marches that I played in the carnival parades. And I played the first one. And they went wild. That's when they start howling, jazz it up again. Oh, yes. It was Chicago who nurtured jazz. Not New Orleans. New Orleans knew little about jazz. I came here in 1925. They had no jazz. Even Sharky was imitating Paul Whiteman. All these boys that talked great, whacked so little, did so much. It's easy when a man organized a club to get all his disgruntled musician who never made good to talk against a man who that did made good. And they have proven every word that I have said it be the truth. And that is the truth. I've been told that they had a man come from California, Gus Miller, who played with Paul Whiteman. He played with Tom Brown. He came here to make a tape record. And when he first came in, he wanted to see me. These are his words he put on his postcard. He says, don't let it fool you by me staying with Tom Brown. I always did admire you and I still admire you. But for money, they'd do anything. I've been told that he's been back here under Dr. Sushant's wing to make a tape recording on jazz. Well, all you had to do is listen to him play with Paul Whiteman and his clarinet. And that's what he played for jazz. You listen to all of them. That takes Nunes. That takes them all in. None of them could play the rhythm. The only time they ever played that rhythm was when I was there hitting, beating down on them and carrying them. And otherwise they couldn't play it. And nobody else played it. Hadn't it been from the men from the north. This would have been a lost art. There wouldn't have been no jazz today. There wouldn't have been no other bands like Tommy Dorsey, Artie Shaw, and the rest of them who came up after in the tea gardens from Texas. Where do you think these people learned their music? Like the New Orleans Rhythm Kings. They played six months out here in Chicago. They made a big affair out of it. Well, they had four boys from the north. Do you think these four boys from New Orleans didn't hear the Dixieland Jazz Band? Armstrong says he did. Armstrong came home with arms full of them. And I can prove he styled himself off the Dixieland Jazz Band. And not only that, the need was stolen all the music that I ever composed. They had taken them part by part and tried to recreate something out of something that I had made out of my own brain. When you wrote the book on this jazz of Joe Oliver, you didn't look up any history at all, did you, Mr. Russ?

No, I wrote that mostly as a sort of, you might say, editor. Walter Allen managed to interview the various musicians that were still living. And he sent me the facts and I wrote them, sewed them up together. I was more concerned with the records than with the legends. I wasn't very interested in these obscure people from the shadows who were said to have played with this, that and the other musician, in this, that and the other band, and who never made any records at all. I'm not interested in music I can't hear and never will hear, after all. I mean, that's dead. That's dead 60 years ago, and it wasn't very interesting anyway. I've heard some of the recreations, some of these records of Bunk Johnson and people like that who were relying on their memories of what they played. Not only was it not jazz, it was barely ragtime. A lot of it was just simply march music, which may have been all right, but I wish they wouldn't label it jazz. It confuses the issue and it just isn't true. When it came to the book, I dug up the files of the various companies and put the pieces together, supplied by Walter Allen, and he did most of the spade work. I just sewed the thing together, and I also managed to get the book published. That was about as far as I went with it.

Now, they say that this, but Freddie Kepit, they make a great big story about it, that he was asked by the Victor Company to record. He says he didn't want to record because he didn't want the world to know his stuff. But they didn't know that I knew all this stuff. They thought that I was just a dumb man, that I didn't know what was going on. They imported them all. The Kepits, the Olivers, and all of them, they all died in the gutter. None of them made good. None of them could make a record. They had to steal the rhythm pattern from the Dixieland Jazz Band and play with younger men to make a record, like Johnny Dodds and Louis Armstrong and the rest, who came after, long ways after. And that's how these old Negroes got by on it. And the legend is that they created this music in the district, in the carnival clubs. No Negro band has ever played, to my knowledge, in the carnival parades. They may have played since I went to New York for these little clubs like the 4th District Club, and the Buzzards and different other small organizations that parade on foot. They may have played there, but they never played no carnival parades, because I played them from 1908 till 1916, and no Negro bands ever played in them parades. Now they give you another laugh about, I see Souchon put out one time, about the burials, and they make so much of them. That is something that the white man had invented thousands of years ago, a military burial. In fact, I myself played many of these funerals. Jack Lane had many funerals he played for, that I was his leader, for the volunteer fire company of Gretna. And there are many note musicians played, these fleas of birds. Oh yeah. That was some of the tunes that we would play, coming to the graveyard, coming back we'd play ragtime music. There was no jazz in New Orleans.

So that the opening words of the late Jelly Roll Morton on his talk for the Library of Congress in Washington, with Alan Lomax, is wrong completely. He says from the very first, the first words he says on those records is, jazz started in New Orleans. And he goes on to tell about how he wrote Tiger Rag, how he named it, and how it was based on the old French quadrilles and all the rest of that stuff. Well, you've told me already, and I believe you absolutely, that that is just so much hooey.
Well, as far as him, he stole his music from the original Dixieland jazz band. You don't have to go any further than that Mellenberg Jaws.
Oh yes.
That's published around 1925.
Great.

This is a Negro who had never been recognized, invented by Alan Lomax. With a few jugs of wine and a couple of needles, furnished by the doctors in New Orleans. He was a set up and tell the history of jazz. A Negro who had never been recognized. Saw what the world broke. Nobody ever listened to him, but Alan Lomax happened to be one of the clique. That is Marshall Starnes, I can name him, for I don't have the list of them. They got a whole bunch of them. They live by piracy and lies. That's all they ever did in their life was lie and live on lies. They didn't come to me and find out what I had to say. Any word that I ever said was always wrong and a lie. And they had men to back them up. Tell them that, well certainly you can back anybody up. In New Orleans is a town, all you got to give them is a few highballs and they're with you. You don't believe me going to a bar room and see two men arguing. Buy them a drink and you write down. Well that's the way New Orleans works. And any time a man of education stoops as low as Dr. Sue Sean and Miss Benville have stooped to blacken a man's character. This has never happened since the time of Christ. Now they don't know me. Yet they were willing to print all untruths. This man Sue Sean gave out articles that Tom Brown was a great man. Well the last words of Tom Brown he tells about the jazz club. He said there was just a bunch of fun loving people who went there to play free music and get drinks. They didn't know nothing about jazz. If you don't believe that, you look in my files when I was to take Tom Jim Brown to court. I'm sorry that I had to do that. But they never stopped at one thing. These men that are so great and big today as historians, they will not put their own name behind it. But they get some poor unfortunate musician who wants to see his name in the paper and they put a statement by him. Now do you like control the press? I don't. Those people control the press. If I went down to Times-Pickey and asked them to put an article in for me, they wouldn't do it. But if the other man like Sue Sean, Miss Manville went around there, they're ready to print it. Whether it was true or not. This is the times we're living in. We're not living in times of honesty anymore. We're living in times of racketeers. Rackets in all lines. And anywhere you take up politics is in it. And the first man to bring this down on me was Marshall Steins. Probably other men had written about it. But he is the one over here that went and got the Guggenheimer Foundation. I think I'm repeating myself on that. I'd like you to say something else in there if you can think of anything.

Well, I don't really think I can, Mr. Rocker. I think that I think I've covered everything. After all, I'm one of those people that just like listening to jazz music. I haven't any sort of first-hand knowledge of what really went on. I wasn't around. I wasn't even born when the first records were made, when jazz was created. But I've done the best I can to catch up with it since. And I was determined to come to the second time I came to New Orleans. I was determined to meet you and to see your files and to have a talk with you.
Well, anyway, what I have wrote to you in my letters, you've checked them.
Yes.
You find that what I have told you. You find that what I have told you. You find that what I have told you.

is the truth absolutely so far yes with the exception of this jelly roll martin who wanted the tutelage of a man who must be communistic or either as an infiltrator of the race hatred now when you come from the south and the man from the south and your man is from the north they think the man from the south mistreats the colored man that is not so there has meant no discrimination against the colored man in my life there's one thing i'd like to say there

it's quite a popular belief i believe that the original dixieland jazz band and you in particular discriminated against the colored people if that is so perhaps some of these people who think themselves so clever and these people who have all the say so in the books and magazines and so on would care to reflect on the number of tunes recorded and played by the original dixieland jazz band that were written by colored men that doesn't look like the discrimination to me think of them there's mammy oh mine by maceo pinkard there was some of these days in the dark town strutters ball by shelton brooks there was jasmine blues by tom delaney there was sister kate by armand pierron i could go on for a long time but they're all written by colored men that doesn't look like

discrimination to me and not only that i played saint louis blues for handy oh yes of course i was forgetting that and our picture was on all these colored publications it was royal garden blues for spencer and clarence that's right spencer claren williams our pictures was on all their publications they were willing to ride our back to get up now that they got up there they tried to bury me but there's two lane archers opened up and i hope to see the future historians and scholars look into the truth and see where that where where this thing has been carried these men who lived on fables who listened to other people everyone was in there to get their share of credit i don't blame them but i blame the men who got all these men together those are the men who have to answer to god why it was done because i can contain no colored men in my band in my youth i never played with colored boys i had no grievance against colored men we lived apart from colored people and colored people lived apart from white we didn't go out and play baseball with colored people we played with white boys boys so did the colored play with their own they may have been some boys down below the section new lanes that mix well i can't tell you much on that because not being down there not being with them i couldn't tell you anything much on that but as far as discriminated against them i have never discriminated against any colored man i played his music as well as i played the white man's music and i made money for them as well as i made it for white men and speaking as a critic i'd like to add just this one

thing before i close that there are recordings made at the same time as yours around 1921 by colored people of numbers like royal garden blues and jasmine blues and i listened to them and they do not contain anything like the same spirit of jazz as yours do they're obviously they're stodgy they're obviously striving after it they're the first attempts to follow and they're trying very hard perhaps they're trying too hard but they don't get there they don't flow they don't move they don't excite the dance anyone to dance they're just nothing and they're by colored bands in 1921 there you see for yourself i can quote from my book if i had it with me the recordings made for columbia of uh mary stafford's jazz band of royal garden blues and crazy blues both numbers which you recorded both written by colored people neither of which in her case neither of her records are of the slightest of interest to jazz jazz at all whereas yours are jazz pure and simple i can say that because i've known the records concern for many years i can i know them note for note well i'm certainly glad that you went through

the uh the victor files because i have known they recorded many of my arguments with the papers and some of these supposed historians that these men recorded they told me no i knew they recorded because

i was told that i would say that the first colored band to make um anything like a jazz record was king oliver's and that wasn't until 1923 seven years later than the first uh no six years later than the first original dixieland jazz band records and then from then on of course uh they started catching on and uh quite a large number of them but up to that time the colored bands were vastly inferior and so

were the white of course now when joe oliver recorded that record there he didn't have everybody from new orleans on that record he had a piano player from tuskegee university oh the little harding i mean that's right he didn't have people from new orleans so you can see that jazz had spread to the four winds then they had men like teak gardens the the byter backs and uh red nickels and uh narvos and all they all coming from all different parts of the country four boys from new orleans going up to chicago meeting other four boys and farming bands the music had become universal by the time joe oliver got to chicago he'd just say he played under the l and did all this kind of stuff he didn't did anything in 1936 he had 10 11 piece band he was leading the band he didn't have a jazz band dan he had a swing band yes he was following the trend each after each white man would white men came into the picture of this thing and synchronized or supposed to synchronize music but he played that's no jazz to me nor me
nor anybody else that knows anything about it i think i don't think then they got this man who

wrote the rapsid in blue he said he got that from the colored man well if you listen up to blue and the blues in the liver stable blues introduction and you got him where he got it mr gushman got it yeah yeah
yeah that uh opening cassette uh gusanda on the clarinet yes i know what you mean exactly that's where he got it

he got he got it enough from no colored man he got it that's where whiteman got all his stuff from that's where whiteman styled his stuff from but he didn't have the rhythm no if you listen to whiteman's record he was a cop in the dixieland jazz band he had bussy there with his buzz tone a couple of little breaks in there and stops and stuff up to that time there was no band that made the different orchestration the same as we made it in other words we were the first one to go out with jazz and have it labeled
by the people of chicago's or jazz band in any case i can certify that the first whiteman recording the very first one of all wasn't made until august the 9th 1920. by that time you'd come back from

england that's right it's a while after that's a good while and they he had all our records oh i expect so all of them so have i well i guess we'll cut this thing short now i'm i thank you ever so much mr and i'm glad you looked to places where i told you and if harry brun had followed my instructions he would have had a better book than he's got now because i want to deal in personalities take these communists down the line these pro negro integrators and tell who they are and bring it down and i hope one day i can live little longer that i can bring this out in public this political system that they use against a man of italian extraction that i it was a miracle that i had to be after the first jazz band it became a miracle they wrote all kinds of history on on mythology something that they didn't know nothing i know sushant ain't old enough to know he'd be old boy i figure how old you think sushant would be 62. if he's 62 and i'm going 70 going to 71. six to seven eight years don't mount mount to much in a man's life let's bring it back to when we were children i was in chicago he was only 17 years old would he know what was going on no he wouldn't know what was going on and no other these guys at 60 and 50 and 40 years old they only taken from what has been written before them and tall lies and legends told by negroes that they did this and anything that had contained syncopation the negro has supposed uh be be the forerunner of syncopation that's not so syncopation has been used for thousands of years by white men the negro never invented syncopation you'll find it in fugues and all dances of away from here uh foreign dance that was brought over imported by the people from europe then they come up with all kinds of talk that the culture this culture what culture the culture they use is what has been taught to them by white people and you go to africa today see what they got culture they're still living in the same way they lived before i think we'll
